finding: The round-2 rewrite of §1 changed 'travels in that report' to the concrete promise that `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence` 'travel in `tp run --status` on any audit-phase stop'. §3.5, also modified this round, enumerates the `tp run --status` payload as a closed list — 'phase, units done, spend against each cap, the last unit's exit code and log path, and `stop_reason`' — which does not include any of the three signals, and §7's `--compact` rule and §10's status test (13) do not mention them either. The repair made §1 a requirement that no other section implements.
suggestion: Add the three divergence signals to §3.5's `tp run --status` payload for audit-phase stops (and state whether they survive `--compact` in §7), and extend §10 test 13 to assert them; otherwise revert §1 to the weaker 'travels in that report' wording.

finding: Test 1 makes the whole loop testable through a fake runner seam named `TP_RUNNER`, but `TP_RUNNER` appears nowhere else in the spec. §3.2 defines the runner purely as a `.tp/config.json` object plus two built-in template names, and §7 lists `runner` as a workflow field resolving CLI > env > task > project > built-in without naming any env variable. So a test author cannot tell whether `TP_RUNNER` is the env layer of the `runner` field (and therefore whether its value is a built-in name, a JSON runner object, or an executable path), or a separate test-only hook that bypasses resolution entirely — and whether it also overrides a per-kind runner map. Every other loop test (2-6, 10-16) is built on this seam, so the ambiguity propagates.
suggestion: Define the seam in §3.2 alongside the runner object: name the variable, state its accepted value form (e.g. path to an executable whose invocations are recorded, or a JSON runner object), state its precedence relative to `runner` and to a per-kind map, and state whether it is honoured outside tests.

finding: "`tp run` holds the same exclusive lock tp's writes take" is not buildable as stated. engine.WithFileLock takes an exclusive flock on the task file's lock path for the duration of fn, and every unit's own tp write (`tp done`, `tp import`, `tp set --workflow`, `tp review --record`) takes that same lock from the child process. If the driver holds it across the run, every child write blocks or exits 4; if it does not, the spec's own duplicate-run guarantee is unbacked. The spec never distinguishes the two locks.
suggestion: Specify a distinct run-scoped lock (e.g. `.tp/locks/run-<task-file>`) that only `tp run` takes, state that the driver holds no lock on the task file itself while children execute, and say which lock produces exit 4 for a second `tp run`.

finding: §3.1 says `tp run` holds the same exclusive lock tp's writes take, for the duration of the run, so that a second `tp run` exits 4. But every unit the driver spawns performs tp writes that take that same lock — `tp done`/`tp commit` (implement), `tp review --record` / `--resolve` (review-record, review-resolve), `tp import` (decompose), `tp audit --record` (audit-record). A parent holding the task-file write lock for the whole run therefore blocks or fails every child it spawns; the mutual-exclusion goal and the child-writes design cannot both hold with one lock.
suggestion: Separate the two locks: `tp run` takes a distinct run-scoped lock (e.g. `.tp/run.lock`) that only excludes other `tp run` invocations over the same task file, and never holds the task-file write lock while a child is in flight. State explicitly that the write lock is taken only by the child commands, for the duration of their own write.

finding: §3.5 was reworded this round to justify `.tp/run.json` as 'one git-ignored progress file that no decision reads back'. §6.2, modified in the same round, then defines the Stop hook's first predicate as 'the run marker is the unit's entry in `.tp/run.json`' — a decision (block or allow the agent to stop) taken by reading that file back. The two modified sections now assert opposite properties of the same file. The schema §3.5 adds makes it worse: the per-unit row carries `exit_code`, `duration_seconds` and `spend_usd`, all of which are only knowable after the child exits, so it is unstated whether the entry the hook needs even exists while the unit is running.
suggestion: Pick one: either state that `.tp/run.json` is written with the unit row at spawn time and narrow the §3.5 claim to 'no *driver* decision reads it back', or give the Stop hook a different marker (an env var the driver sets, or a per-unit marker file) so §3.5's no-readback property survives intact.

finding: §6.2's Stop hook predicate is "the run marker is the unit's entry in `.tp/run.json`", which requires the row to exist *before* the child runs; but §3.5's row schema is entirely post-hoc (`exit_code`, `duration_seconds`, `spend_usd`). The spec never says when rows are written (pre-spawn placeholder then updated on exit? only on exit?), nor what the pre-spawn row's `exit_code`/`duration_seconds` hold, nor whether `.tp/run.json` is rewritten atomically while concurrent role children may be reading it.
suggestion: State the write points explicitly: a row is appended before the child is spawned with null exit_code/duration/spend, and updated in place after it exits; writes are atomic (temp+rename) because hooks in concurrent children read the file.

finding: `last_failure` is cleared by 'a success clears it only when `unit_id` matches', but §3.1 says unit ids are unique only *within a run*, and both record kinds use the same id space: 'the round number for a record unit' covers `review-record` and `audit-record`. A successful `audit-record` for round 2 therefore clears a `last_failure` written by a failed `review-record` round 2 (and the object survives across runs by design, so cross-run collisions on task ids and finding indices are possible too). The stored object already carries `unit_kind` and `phase`, so the clearing predicate contradicts the data it stores. A tester cannot write test 7's 'cleared on the next success of that unit' without picking a key, and two engineers will pick different ones.
suggestion: State the clearing key explicitly as the tuple that identifies a unit — `(unit_kind, unit_id)` at minimum, `(phase, unit_kind, unit_id)` if phase participates — and add a test that a same-id different-kind success does not clear it.

finding: §4.2 and test 7 both require `last_failure` to be surfaced by '`tp resume` and `tp brief`', but `tp brief` is not an existing tp command (REFERENCE.md documents `brief_command` as a per-phase command name and `tp next --brief` as a flag), and this spec introduces no `tp brief` command anywhere — §3.2 and §4.1 only reference the oracle-supplied `brief_command`. Test 7 as written pins a surface that does not exist and that the spec does not create, so it cannot be executed as stated.
suggestion: Either name the actual surfaces (`tp resume` and every `brief_command` output — `tp next --brief`, `tp review`, `tp audit`), or, if a new `tp brief` command is intended, specify it in §3/§4 with its arguments and output before test 7 relies on it.

finding: The round-2 rewrite makes the escalating unit — a child process — the writer of `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json`, and makes the presence of that record, not the exit code, the signal that distinguishes an escalation from a unit failure. But §3.2's placeholder set is `{prompt}`, `{max_budget_usd}`, `{unit_id}`, `{log_path}`, and the only environment the spec gives the child is `TP_UNATTENDED`; `TP_RUN_ID` is described as an environment variable for `notify_cmd`, not for the unit. Nothing tells the child what `<run-id>` is, so as written the unit cannot construct the path the driver looks at, and every escalation degrades into an ordinary `unit-failure`.
suggestion: Name the channel that carries the run id into the child — e.g. export `TP_RUN_ID` (and the run directory) to every unit alongside `TP_UNATTENDED`, or add a `{run_dir}` placeholder — and say which tp command writes the record so the unit is not hand-constructing the path.

finding: The unit is named as the writer of `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json`, but nothing in the spec lets it write one: the child is never given the run id, there is no `tp escalate` command, and the record's field vocabulary is undefined (`decision` — a free string or one of §5.1's three refusals? `options[]` — strings or objects? `evidence` — how bounded?). The driver's behaviour on a present-but-malformed record is also unstated, and §5.2 makes that file the difference between `escalation` and `unit-failure`.
suggestion: Add a `tp escalate --decision … --evidence … [--option …]` command (or an exact documented path + schema plus a `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` env var), enumerate `decision` values, and state that an unparseable or schema-invalid record is treated as an ordinary unit failure.

finding: §5.2 claims "At most one record is written per run; a second escalation in the same run cannot occur, because the first stops it." That reasoning only holds for serialized units. §3.1 step 4 spawns role units concurrently and §3.4 states caps and stops are evaluated between iterations while "children already spawned run to completion" — so two sibling role units in the same iteration can both escalate, and both write the single fixed path `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json`. The uniqueness claim is false and the write is a lost-update race on one file.
suggestion: Either make the escalation record per-unit (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-escalation.json`) and define which one the driver reports when an iteration produces several, or state that the driver, not the unit, writes the single record after collecting the iteration's results — and drop the "cannot occur" claim in favour of a first-writer-wins rule with the losers recorded.

finding: §5.2 now fixes the escalation record at a single per-run path `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json` and asserts 'At most one record is written per run; a second escalation in the same run cannot occur, because the first stops it'. That reasoning assumes one unit in flight, but §3.1 step 4 and §3.3 spawn all sibling role units of an iteration concurrently, and §3.4 says in-flight children run to completion. Two concurrent `review-role`/`audit-role` units that both hit a user-only decision write the same fixed path in the same iteration; the second silently overwrites the first, and the operator loses one escalation.
suggestion: Either scope the record per unit (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-escalation.json`) and have the driver stop on the first one it observes while preserving all of them, or state that a concurrent sibling's escalation write must not clobber an existing record (create-exclusive, first writer wins) and drop the 'cannot occur' claim.

finding: The Stop hook cannot be built from what is given. (a) It has no way to know which unit it is inside — no unit id, run id or seq is stated to reach the child's environment or cwd (§3.2 only lists `{unit_id}`/`{log_path}` as *argv* placeholders for the runner, which the hook cannot see). (b) "the durable write is the artifact its kind names in §3.3" points at prose outcomes ("One task committed and closed", "The spec revised and each addressed finding resolved"), not at checkable paths; for `review-resolve` and `decompose` there is no artifact path anywhere in the spec.
suggestion: Export `TP_RUN_ID`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_UNIT_KIND` and `TP_UNIT_SEQ` into every child (after the runner.env merge, like TP_UNATTENDED), and give §3.3 a fourth column naming the exact durable-write predicate per kind (path or state assertion) that both the driver and the Stop hook evaluate.

finding: The `Stop` hook blocks when "the run marker is present and the unit's durable write is absent". §5.2 defines escalation as "a normal, expected outcome — not a crash", and an escalating unit by definition produces no durable write; the same is true of a unit that legitimately fails and exits non-zero (§4.2). So the hook blocks precisely the two outcomes the spec designs for, forcing an extra turn out of an agent that already did the right thing, and — for an escalation — risking the unit doing something else instead of exiting 2.
suggestion: Give the hook a third predicate: do not block when an escalation record for this unit exists, and do not block when the unit is exiting non-zero (or state that the hook only fires on a zero-exit stop). Add a test to §10 alongside test 10 covering an escalating unit under the Stop hook.

finding: Two different filenames are specified for the same artifact: §6.3 pins the role's findings file at `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<role>.ndjson`, while the prompt `tp review`/`tp audit` already emits (which §6.3 says is the durable contract) tells the role to write its own filename such as `review-r2-implementer.ndjson`. An implementer cannot satisfy both. The record unit's side is also missing: nothing says how `review-record`/`audit-record` discovers the current round's role files (the run dir accumulates every round's files and the record unit does not know the sibling seqs), or where the merged output is written.
suggestion: Pick one path owner. Either make `tp review`/`tp audit` emit the `.tp/runs/<run-id>/` path in the prompt, or drop §6.3's path and let the agent's write allowlist match the emitted filename; then state the round-scoped glob (e.g. `.tp/runs/<run-id>/r<round>-<role>.ndjson`) and the merged file's path that the record unit consumes.

finding: Test 21, '`next_action`'s mechanize branch carries the phase qualifier', pins nothing observable: §8a describes the qualifier only in prose ('it names the class and states that a check is worth registering only when the artifact it measures already exists in the review phase'), and does not say whether the qualifier is a new JSON field, a substring of an existing `summary`/`command`, or free text. Two engineers write contradictory assertions (one greps a substring that any rewording breaks, the other asserts a field that does not exist).
suggestion: Pin the observable in §8a: either name the JSON field the qualifier occupies and its shape, or quote the exact sentence the emitter produces, and have test 21 assert that.

finding: Test 5 — 'Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them' — names no observable, so the assertion is either non-deterministic (comparing wall-clock start/end stamps recorded by the fake runner, which flakes on a loaded machine) or vacuous. §3.3 states the property and its bound ('bounded by the number of active roles for the phase') but never says what the driver records that makes concurrency visible: `.tp/run.json`'s unit rows carry `duration_seconds` but no start timestamp, so overlap cannot even be derived from the run state.
suggestion: Pin a deterministic observable — e.g. the fake runner blocks on a barrier and the test asserts N role children are in-flight simultaneously before any is released, and that a non-role unit's child is never spawned while another child is live — and, if run state is to be the evidence, add a start timestamp to the unit row in §3.5.

finding: Test 6 asserts 'A crashed driver loses nothing: a second `tp run` over the same state resumes at the same unit', but §3.1 pins the crash observable for exactly one of the eight kinds ('A crashed `implement` unit leaves its task `wip`; the next run's `implement` unit resumes that same task'). For the other seven the spec says nothing about the mid-write state: a `review-record` killed after merging but before recording, an `audit-role` killed after writing half its NDJSON, a `review-resolve` killed after revising the spec but before resolving findings. A tester cannot write 'resumes at the same unit' for those without inventing the partial-state semantics, and the test as worded implies all kinds.
suggestion: Either scope test 6 to the kinds whose crash semantics §3.1 pins, or add to §3.1 what each kind leaves behind on a mid-unit crash and which of those partial artifacts the next run must discard versus resume from (in particular a half-written role findings file).

finding: §3.2 makes `runner` take one of three shapes (built-in name, runner object, per-kind map with a mandatory `default` key), makes a map missing `default` a usage error, and makes the budget flag appended only when `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is non-zero (with a 0 omitting the flag rather than passing a literal 0); §7 repeats '0 (flag omitted)'. Test 14 covers placeholder resolution only and test 15 covers spend only, so nothing in §10 pins runner-shape resolution, the missing-`default` usage error, the per-kind map that the whole producer/judge separation argument in §3.2 rests on, or the flag-omission boundary at exactly 0 (the case a mutation on `>` vs `>=` would survive).
suggestion: Add tests: each of the three runner shapes resolves for a given unit kind; a per-kind map without `default` exits 2 before any spawn; `run_max_unit_budget_usd` of 0 produces argv without the budget flag while the smallest non-zero value produces it; and a per-kind map routes an `audit-role` unit to a different `cmd` from an `implement` unit.

finding: §5.1 defines unattended mode by a three-part predicate — the variable is 'present, non-empty and not `0`' — but test 8 exercises only `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and the variable absent. The two boundary values that distinguish the predicate from a plain presence check (empty string, literal `0`) are untested, as are the near-miss forms an operator will actually produce (`00`, `false`, ` 0 `), whose treatment the spec does not state either. This is exactly the shape the mutation-testing lesson names: a behavioural test that verifies a rule while missing its boundary.
suggestion: State how the value is normalised (trimmed? only the exact string `0` disables?), then extend test 8 to assert mode inactive for empty and `0`, active for `1`, `true` and any other non-empty value, and pin whichever of `00`/`false`/whitespace-padded forms the normalisation rule implies.

finding: The unit-id paragraph added this round claims 'Ids are unique within a run and are what `last_failure` clears on'. The id assignment it gives makes that false for role units: a `review-role`/`audit-role` unit's id is the role id, and every review or audit round of the same run re-runs the same fixed corpus of roles, so `implementer` (or `spec-coverage`) recurs once per round within one run. `implement` ids likewise recur when a crashed task is resumed in the same run. §3.5's schema already carries `seq` precisely because the id is not unique.
suggestion: Replace 'unique within a run' with the property actually needed — 'stable for the same subject, so a retry and a later attempt at the same subject share an id; `seq` is what distinguishes executions' — and state explicitly that `last_failure` clearing on a repeated id is intended.

finding: §4.1 was repaired this round to drop the per-entry `concurrent` field: 'Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table'. §3.1 step 4, modified in the same round, still reads 'units marked concurrent together, every other kind alone', which describes a per-unit mark that §4.1 explicitly removed. A reader implementing §3.1 looks for a mark that the oracle no longer emits.
suggestion: Reword §3.1 step 4 to derive concurrency from the kind, e.g. 'Spawn a runner process per unit — units whose kind §3.3 marks parallel together, every other kind alone'.

finding: Round 1 described the `claude` template abstractly ('print mode with streaming JSON output, `--permission-mode auto`, and the per-unit turn and budget caps'). The round-2 repair replaced that with a literal argv — `["-p", "{prompt}", "--output-format", "stream-json", "--verbose", "--permission-mode", "auto"]` plus `["--max-budget-usd", "{max_budget_usd}"]`, and `["run", "{prompt}"]` for opencode. These are third-party CLI surfaces whose correctness cannot be established against this spec at all, only against the installed harness, and they drift the moment either CLI changes a flag. That is the altitude a task's acceptance owns, not the spec's.
suggestion: Keep the properties that are tp's decisions in §3.2 — stdin closed, streaming JSON to the log, non-interactive permission handling, per-unit budget flag appended only when non-zero, no budget flag for opencode — and move the exact argv into the acceptance of the task that ships the templates, where it can be verified against the installed CLI.

finding: The `args` template defines four placeholders but neither shipped template consumes `{unit_id}` or `{log_path}`: `claude` uses `{prompt}` and `{max_budget_usd}`, `opencode` uses `{prompt}` alone. `{log_path}` additionally overlaps the driver's own behaviour — §3.5 has the driver streaming the child's output to that path itself, so a runner writing its own log there is unspecified and possibly conflicting. Both placeholders carry cost: resolution machinery, the exit-2 unresolved-placeholder path, and test 14.
suggestion: Ship only the placeholders a built-in template uses (`{prompt}`, `{max_budget_usd}`) and add the others when a runner needs them; or name the consumer each one exists for and, for `{log_path}`, say whether the child writes that file or the driver does.

finding: The spend behaviour added this round names the reported field two different ways. §3.2 says a runner declaring no `spend_key` 'reports `spend: null` for its units' and §10 test 15 says it 'reports `spend` null', while §3.5's new `.tp/run.json` schema — the only place the field is actually defined — calls it `spend_usd` in both the per-unit row and `totals`. Nothing in the spec introduces a separate `spend` field, so one of the two names is wrong.
suggestion: Use `spend_usd` in §3.2 and §10 test 15 to match §3.5's schema (or rename the schema field), and say once which object the reported value lands in.

finding: The spend read has no error path. A child that crashes may leave an empty file, a truncated final line, non-JSON output, or valid JSON without the declared `spend_key`. The spec says only that a runner declaring no key reports `spend: null`. It does not say whether an unreadable/absent value is `null`, whether it counts as 0 against `run_max_budget_usd` (silently letting a budgeted run overshoot), or whether it makes the unit a failed attempt.
suggestion: State: a missing, unparseable or non-numeric spend value yields `spend: null`, contributes 0 to the accrued total, is never a unit failure on its own, and is surfaced once in `tp run --status` so a budgeted run cannot appear to be within a cap it stopped measuring.

finding: "the finding index for `audit-fix`" is not a defined identifier. Audit rows have carried stable slug ids (`file-<role>-<slug>`, v0.30.0) precisely because positional indices were unstable, and the spec does not say what the index counts (rows in the merged results file? non-PASS rows only? per role?), nor whether it must remain stable across rounds so `last_failure` clears on a matching `unit_id`.
suggestion: Use the audit row's existing stable id as the `audit-fix` unit id and say so, or define the index's derivation and its stability guarantee explicitly.

finding: `audit-fix` is scoped to one audit finding per unit (its id is 'the finding index', §3.1) and runs Alone, while `review-resolve` batches every addressed finding for a spec into a single unit. A round with 20 audit findings therefore costs 20 serialized fresh processes, each paying full context startup (read spec, read the relevant code, run the gate, commit) for one small edit, and can consume a fifth of the default `run_max_units` of 100 in one round. The same work in the review phase costs one unit. This breaks P2 batch parity in the phase most likely to produce many small items, and the per-unit cost is context startup, which is exactly what this version exists to economize.
suggestion: Make `audit-fix` batch the same way `review-resolve` does — one unit per audit round whose id is the round number, fixing the round's recorded findings and committing per finding — or state a bounded fan-out (e.g. one unit per file or per role) and justify why per-finding startup is worth paying. If per-finding really is required, say what decision the finer granularity feeds that a per-round unit could not.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" is not placed in the loop of §3.1. Two consequences are undefined: whether a retry is an in-iteration respawn or a new iteration (which decides whether caps, evaluated "between iterations only", can trip between attempts and whether the driver re-reads cycle state first — it must, since a partially completed attempt changes what the retry should do), and whether each attempt counts toward `run_max_units`/`cap-units`. §3.5's per-unit `attempt` field suggests one row per attempt, which would make retries consume the unit cap, but `totals.units` is never defined against it. For a concurrent role batch, whether a failed member is retried alone or with the batch is also unstated.
suggestion: Define the retry as a fresh iteration over re-read state, say explicitly whether an attempt increments `totals.units` and `cap-units`, and state that a failed member of a concurrent batch is retried alone while its successful siblings are not re-run.

finding: "`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` set `interrupted` on the same terms: in-flight children finish" is not achievable by default. A ^C from a terminal is delivered to the whole foreground process group, so children receive SIGINT too and die rather than finishing, unless the driver spawns them in their own process group (Setpgid). The spec never states that requirement, so the implementer must guess.
suggestion: State that children are spawned in a new process group with stdin closed, that the driver does not forward signals to them, and that the driver waits for in-flight children before writing the run state on interrupt.

finding: §8a makes it a required behaviour that "a driver can separate a mistyped invocation from a failed one without reading the message", yet `tp run`'s own exit codes are given only for two cases: exit 0 on `converged` (§3.1 step 2) and exit 4 on a concurrent run (§3.1). The other seven `stop_reason` values in §3.4's table have no exit code, so the very tool a cron or CI trigger invokes (§9 Non-Goal 3) has no machine-readable outcome — and the existing table (0 success, 1 validation, 2 usage, 3 file, 4 state) has no obvious slot for `cap-units` versus `unit-failure` versus `escalation`.
suggestion: Add an exit-code column to §3.4's table (or a paragraph after it) mapping every `stop_reason` to a code, keeping the existing five-code contract intact, and add a §10 test asserting the mapping for each reason.

finding: §3.5 justifies `.tp/run.json` as "observability, not truth" on the ground that it is "one git-ignored progress file that no decision reads back". §6.2's Stop hook reads it back and makes a decision from it: "the run marker is the unit's entry in `.tp/run.json`". Beyond the contradiction, the write timing is unspecified and the schema argues against the hook working at all: a unit row carries `exit_code`, `duration_seconds` and `spend_usd`, values that only exist after the child exits, while the Stop hook fires while the child is still running — so the marker the hook needs may not be in the file yet.
suggestion: State when the driver writes each unit row (append a row with `attempt`/`kind`/`id`/`log_path` before spawning, complete it on exit), and reword §3.5 to say no *convergence or scheduling* decision reads it back, acknowledging the hook as a reader.

finding: §4.1 says of `next_units`: "The array is the machine surface, and the only field the driver parses." The same section then makes releasability depend on another field — "The cycle is releasable when `phase` is `release`" — which the driver must parse to implement §3.1 step 2. §1 adds that `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence` travel in `tp run --status`, and §3.5 has `--status` print the phase, so the driver reads those too.
suggestion: Replace "the only field the driver parses" with the accurate set: `next_units` is the only field the driver *dispatches* on; `phase` decides releasability and the divergence signals are passed through to `--status` unread. Name that set explicitly so a later change cannot silently widen it.

finding: §4.1 states two oracle-side invariants the driver depends on but §10 pins neither: 'a non-concurrent kind is never returned alongside another unit' (without which §3.1 step 4 spawns concurrent writers, contradicting Non-Goal 5), and '`next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` render `next_units[0]` when the array is non-empty' (the consistency between the human and machine surfaces). Test 2 only asserts the loop advances through phases; §10.1 only notes that assertions pinning `tp resume`'s object set must move.
suggestion: Add a test asserting `next_units` never mixes a non-concurrent kind with any sibling and returns only same-kind role units when it returns more than one, and a test asserting `next_action.command`/`brief_command`/`payload` equal the `next_units[0]` rendering in each phase (and what they hold when `next_units` is empty).

finding: §4.2 clears `last_failure` "only when `unit_id` matches", and §3.1 asserts ids are unique within a run. The id definitions make that untrue across kinds: a record unit's id is the round number and an `audit-fix` unit's id is the finding index, so review round 2 and audit round 2 both have id `2`, and finding index 3 recurs in every round. A successful `audit-record` for round 2 would therefore clear a `last_failure` written by a failed `review-record` for round 2. §3.5's log path `<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` already concedes that `id` alone does not identify a unit.
suggestion: Make the clearing key `(unit_kind, unit_id)` everywhere `last_failure` is matched, and either qualify the round/finding ids (e.g. `review-r2`, `audit-r2`, `audit-fix-r3-7`) or restate the uniqueness claim as unique per `(kind, id)` within a run.

finding: §5.2 gained the rule that an escalating unit 'is not counted as a failed attempt, and does not set `last_failure`'. §4.2, rewritten in the same round, states the general rule without that carve-out: 'When a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate, tp records a `last_failure` object'. An escalating unit exits 2 — non-zero — so the two modified sections prescribe opposite behaviour for the same event, and §10's tests assert both (test 7 the general rule, test 10 the exception) without noting which wins.
suggestion: Add the exception to §4.2 where the rule is stated: 'except a unit that exits 2 having written an escalation record (§5.2), which sets no `last_failure`'.

finding: §5.1's fence covers `--skip-gate`, raising `review_max_rounds`/`audit_max_rounds`, and `import --force`, on the stated rationale that "tp's equivalent of a forged approval is an agent that raises its own round budget". The seven fields §7 adds are writable by the same `tp set --workflow` route and have exactly that shape: an unattended unit can raise `run_max_units`, `run_max_wall_clock_seconds` or `run_max_budget_usd` and extend the run that is supervising it. The spec also never says whether the driver snapshots the caps at run start or re-resolves them each iteration, which decides whether such a write takes effect at all.
suggestion: Add the `run_max_*` caps to §5.1's fail-closed table on the same equal-or-lower rule, and state in §3.4 that caps are resolved once at run start and held for the run (which makes a mid-run raise inert and the fence a belt-and-braces).

finding: The escalation record is a 7-key schema (`{decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at}`) the *unit* must author, yet everything in it is already known to tp at the moment of refusal: §5.1's refusal produces the decision and hint, and `unit_kind`/`unit_id`/`phase` are what the driver stamped and what `last_failure` (§4.2) already records. The spec's own routing — 'a tp command that refuses under §5.1 prints the hint and the unit records the escalation from it' — spends a round-trip having the agent transcribe tp's own output back into a file, which inverts P4 (agent plans, tool executes) on the most safety-relevant path in the version, and makes the signal depend on the agent transcribing correctly. The driver then reads none of the fields; it only checks the file exists and hands its path to `notify_cmd`.
suggestion: Have the refusing tp command write `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json` itself (it knows the decision, the attempted value, the phase, and can read the unit id from the driver's environment), leaving the unit only to exit. If a unit must be able to escalate for a non-tp reason, keep an agent-writable form with two fields (`decision`, `evidence`) and let tp fill the rest.

finding: §6.1 makes the plugin preflight a hard behaviour: if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than the minimum it 'fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly', and the minimum is `plugin.json`'s own version compared against `tp --version`. §10's only plugin tests are 17 (`claude plugin validate` plus hook payload fixtures) and 18 (the `PreToolUse` deny), neither of which touches the preflight. Version comparison is exactly the code that needs a boundary test (equal version, one patch below, a pre-release or dev suffix from a `go build` binary), and none is pinned.
suggestion: Add a test that the preflight fails with the install command when `tp` is absent and when `tp --version` is below `plugin.json`'s version, passes at exactly that version, and specify how a non-release version string (e.g. `dev`, `0.35.0-rc1`) compares.

finding: Of §6.2's three hooks only the `PreToolUse` deny is tested (test 18). The `Stop` hook carries the version's most dangerous failure mode in its own words — 'A hook that always blocks produces an agent that can never finish' — and its two predicates (the unit's entry in `.tp/run.json` as run marker, the kind's durable write from §3.3) plus the `stop_hook_active` consult and 'block at most once per unit' rule are unverified; the `SessionStart` hook's requirement that its payload be `tp resume --compact` 'and nothing else', on every matcher, is likewise unverified. Test 17's 'hook payloads are asserted against fixtures' names no hook and no assertion, so it cannot stand in for either. §6.4's 10-second `timeout` on every shipped hook is also unpinned.
suggestion: Add tests: the `Stop` hook blocks exactly once when the marker is present and the durable write is missing, does not block when the durable write exists, and does not block when `stop_hook_active` is set; the `SessionStart` hook injects the `tp resume --compact` payload and nothing else for every matcher; every shipped hook declares `timeout: 10`.

finding: The `SessionStart` hook injects `tp resume --compact` into every child session on every matcher. Under `tp run` — the mode this version exists for — the driver has already chosen the unit and §3.2's `{prompt}` tells the child to run its own `brief_command` and stop; the child never decides what phase the cycle is in or what runs next. So the orientation payload is not 'occasionally redundant', it is redundant on every one of up to `run_max_units` (default 100) child processes, and it partly duplicates what the brief then emits. §6.2's own defence of not branching on the matcher argues about clear-vs-startup, not about the brief overlap.
suggestion: Either suppress the SessionStart injection when `TP_UNATTENDED` is set (the driver already stamps it, §5.1) and keep it for interactive sessions where the operator does choose the next step, or state what the injected orientation gives an unattended unit that its own `brief_command` does not — and trim the payload to that part.

finding: §6.3 lets `tp-reviewer` and `tp-auditor` write "exactly one path" — their findings file — and denies every other write. §5.2 obliges any unit that needs a user-only decision to write `.tp/runs/<run-id>/escalation.json`, so a role unit that must escalate is denied its only supported exit. Separately, the allowed path `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<role>.ndjson` contains two values (`<run-id>`, `<seq>`) that do not exist when the static agent definition is written, so the definition can only express it as a glob — which the spec should say, since a loose glob re-opens the directory it is fencing.
suggestion: Add `escalation.json` under the current run directory to both roles' write allowlist, and state the exact glob form the agent definitions use for the findings path.

finding: §6.3 now pins the role findings path to `.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<role>.ndjson`, 'which the `review-record` and `audit-record` units then read and merge'. Two inputs in that path are the driver's private numbering: `<run-id>` and `<seq>`. As with §5.2, no placeholder or environment variable is stated that would let a role unit know its own `<seq>`, and nothing tells the record unit which sibling files belong to the round it is recording (roles from an earlier round of the same run sit in the same directory under lower seq numbers). Round 1's looser 'each writes only its own file' had no such dependency.
suggestion: Either give the record unit a round-scoped directory (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/round-<n>/<role>.ndjson`) so the merge glob is unambiguous, or state the placeholder/env channel that carries `<seq>` to the role unit and the rule the record unit uses to select the current round's files.

finding: The only `--compact` rule in the spec covers run status ('stop_reason and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped'). Three new payload additions get no compact behaviour: `next_units` (§4.1), `location_clusters` (§8a) and `file_summary`'s new keys (§8a). This matters concretely because §6.2 injects `tp resume --compact` into every child session, so an unspecified compact rule for `next_units` means an array of `{kind, id, brief_command}` may land in every unit's context — where the driver, not the unit, is the consumer.
suggestion: State the compact rule for each new key: strip `next_units` from `--compact` (the driver never asks for compact output) and strip `location_clusters` unless a human is reading, keeping the aggregate count. Add an assertion to §10 that `tp resume --compact` does not carry `next_units`.

finding: `notify_cmd` is "read from `.tp/local.json` only", but `.tp/local.json` currently holds an `active` pointer and a CLI-flag `defaults` map, and the spec gives no key placement (top-level `notify_cmd`? inside `defaults`?), no validation rule, and no reconciliation with the sentence one paragraph later saying `tp config --resolved`, `--extract` and `validate --project` cover the new fields "on the same terms" — `validate --project` validates project config, which `notify_cmd` explicitly is not.
suggestion: Name the exact `.tp/local.json` key and value type, and say explicitly which of the three config commands report `notify_cmd` and which ignore it (e.g. shown by `--resolved`, never emitted by `--extract`, out of scope for `validate --project`).

finding: §3.2 states `runner` "takes one of three shapes: a built-in template name, a runner object, or a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key", and devotes a paragraph to why the per-kind map matters (producer/judge separation). §7's table, which is the normative field surface `tp config --resolved` and `tp validate --project` validate against, gives `runner`'s Range as "Built-in name or object" — the third shape is missing, so a validator written from §7 rejects the map §3.2 requires.
suggestion: Extend §7's Range cell to "Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map with `default`", and say there that a map missing `default` is a usage error (currently only in §3.2).

finding: `location_clusters` is added to both `tp review --merge` and `--status` output, and the same paragraph states it is 'reporting only: convergence arithmetic, the stored `clean` flag and the `--status --check` exit code are unchanged'. The measured defect it is answering is that an unattended driver reads a merged count as rounds remaining — but the driver's count, flag and exit code are all untouched, so the new key changes no driver decision and the defect it names is unfixed. It is a new per-location object `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` emitted on every merge and every status call for a human to interpret.
suggestion: Either give the cluster data a decision to feed (e.g. report it only in `--status` where the operator reads it, or let `next_action` reference it), or drop the emitted key and state the clustered-count caveat in `next_action.summary`/the docs instead. If it stays, scope it to `--status` only so `--merge`'s per-round output does not grow.

finding: `location_clusters` on `tp review --status` has no defined input. A recorded round stores only `{round, findings, clean, file, …}` (engine.ReviewRound), so `--status` would have to re-read each round's recorded file. The spec does not say which round(s) `--status` clusters, whether an in-flight round with role files but no record is included, or what happens when a recorded file's rows carry no `role` field (hand-authored or pre-v0.35 merges), which silently yields zero clusters for a round that has them.
suggestion: State that `--status` clusters the latest recorded round by re-reading its `file`, that rows lacking `role` are excluded and counted in a `clustering_skipped` number, and whether an in-flight round contributes.

finding: §8a's arity paragraph says every command's `Args` validator exits 2, "matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is Non-Goals and defines nothing about usage errors — its seven items are the memory layer, self-clear, scheduler, convergence policy, parallel writing units, prose parsing and decomposition semantics. The only place in this spec that fixes exit 2 as a usage error is §3.2 ("A placeholder the driver cannot resolve is a usage error (exit 2)"); the authoritative table lives in `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`.
suggestion: Point the reference at the exit-code table in REFERENCE.md (or at §3.2), not at §9.

finding: Test 2 says the loop 'advances through implement, review and audit phases', but the cycle order the rest of the spec assumes is review -> decompose -> implement -> audit -> release (§3.3's kind table and §4.1's phases), and `decompose` — a unit kind with its own row — is omitted from the list. A tester following test 2 literally builds a fixture in the wrong order and never exercises the decompose transition, which is the one phase whose `next_action.command` is null in the existing oracle.
suggestion: Reword test 2 to name the phases in cycle order and include decompose, e.g. 'the loop advances review -> decompose -> implement -> audit and stops with `converged` when the oracle reports `phase` `release`', and assert the unit kind executed in each phase.

finding: §3.1 step 4 says "units marked concurrent together", implying a per-unit marker; §4.1 says the opposite — "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table" — and the `next_units` entry shape `{kind, id, brief_command}` carries no such mark.
suggestion: Reword step 4 as "units whose kind §3.3 marks parallel are spawned together; every other kind alone".

finding: The overshoot paragraph added this round says 'a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration'. `run_max_units` is subject to the same effect and is omitted: caps are evaluated between iterations, and an iteration spawns every sibling role unit at once, so a run with `run_max_units` one below the boundary executes the whole fan-out before `cap-units` trips.
suggestion: Say that all three quantitative caps — units, wall clock and budget — can overshoot by at most one iteration, and that the iteration is the granularity because the driver kills nothing.

finding: The overshoot sentence covers only wall-clock and budget, but `run_max_units` overshoots on the same terms: an iteration spawning N parallel role units can cross `run_max_units` by up to N-1 since caps are evaluated between iterations. An implementer reading the cap table literally would try to stop mid-iteration.
suggestion: Extend the sentence to name `run_max_units` (a run can exceed it by at most one iteration's unit count), or state that the driver trims the last iteration's unit list to fit the cap.

finding: The `.tp/run.json` unit rows store `log_path`, which §3.5 already defines as a pure function of the run id, seq, kind and id (`.tp/runs/<run-id>/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`), and `totals` stores counts that the `units` array already determines. For a run at the default cap that is 100 stored paths plus three stored aggregates in a file the spec itself says 'no decision reads back'.
suggestion: Drop `log_path` from the unit rows and state the path rule once, or keep the path and drop `seq`/`kind`/`id` duplication. Either compute `totals` at read time for `--status` or say explicitly that they are a crash-resilience cache, since §3.5 otherwise argues against exactly this kind of second copy.

finding: `next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` are specified to render `next_units[0]`, so every `tp resume --json` emits the first unit's command and brief command twice. The array is 'the machine surface, and the only field the driver parses'; the mirrored copy exists for a human who is, in the unattended path, not reading the JSON at all.
suggestion: Keep `next_action` as prose only (`summary` plus a pointer to `next_units[0]`) rather than re-rendering its command fields, or state that `next_action`'s command fields are omitted whenever `next_units` is non-empty.

finding: "The minimum is `plugin.json`'s own version, compared against `tp --version`" makes every plugin release pin an equal-or-newer binary in lockstep: a plugin bumped to 0.36.0 for a hook or doc change refuses to run against a perfectly capable tp 0.35.0. The plugin and the binary ship through different channels (git marketplace vs Homebrew/`go install`, §6.1), so they will routinely be at different versions.
suggestion: Carry an explicit `min_tp_version` field in `plugin.json`, bumped only when the plugin actually requires new binary behaviour, rather than deriving the minimum from the plugin's own version.

finding: §5.1's restrictions are explicitly gated on `TP_UNATTENDED`, but §6.2's `PreToolUse` denial has no such gate: any session with the plugin installed loses `Write`/`Edit` on `.tp/config.json` and `.tp/local.json`. §8 keeps interactive, human-supervised sessions as a supported fallback, and editing project config is a normal thing to do in one (CLAUDE.md's own v0.24.0 migration is exactly that edit). The spec never acknowledges that the plugin changes interactive behaviour.
suggestion: Either scope the config-file rows of the deny list to unattended sessions, or state deliberately that the denial is unconditional and name the supported interactive route for editing those files (`tp set --workflow` / `tp config --extract` / `tp use`).

finding: `run_max_budget_usd` and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` are two budget knobs where the run-level one pulls in an entire apparatus for a bound the other already implies: `spend_key` config, per-unit `spend_usd` (nullable), `totals.spend_usd`, null-spend semantics, the 'reported once at run start, not silently' notice, `cap-budget`, and test 15 — and it is inert for one of the two shipped runners (`opencode` declares no `spend_key`). `run_max_units` × `run_max_unit_budget_usd` already gives an operator a hard ceiling with no log parsing at all.
suggestion: Ship `run_max_unit_budget_usd` (the runner's own flag, passed through) plus `run_max_units` as the spend bound, and defer `run_max_budget_usd`, `spend_key` and `cap-budget` until a runner-agnostic cost source exists — or justify the run-level cap by naming a decision the per-unit cap cannot bound.

finding: §7 is 'Workflow fields', and the round-2 revision appended 'Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped' to it. That is a rule about `tp run --status` output, whose payload §3.5 defines; a reader looking for the status contract will not find it under workflow field resolution, and §3.5 gives no forward pointer.
suggestion: Move the `--compact` sentence to §3.5 next to the `tp run --status` payload, keeping §7 to field defaults, ranges and the resolution path.

finding: §7 opens with "New project-level defaults, resolving at read time through the existing layered path" and then exempts `notify_cmd` as per-operator, read from `.tp/local.json` only. The following paragraph then re-includes it: "`tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields on the same terms as every existing workflow field." `--extract` writes project config and `--project` validates it, so both are meaningless for a local-only field.
suggestion: Qualify the coverage sentence to exclude `notify_cmd` from `--extract`/`--project`, and say where it does surface (e.g. `tp config --resolved` with a local-only marker).

finding: §7 pins a `--compact` contract for the run surface — 'Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped' — and that `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the seven new fields on the same terms as existing workflow fields, including their ranges (e.g. `run_max_units` 1-10000, `run_max_unit_retries` 0-5) and the `notify_cmd` exception that resolves from `.tp/local.json` only. Test 13 covers `tp run --status` without mentioning `--compact`, and no test covers the config/validate surface or the range boundaries.
suggestion: Add a test that `tp run --status --compact` keeps `stop_reason` and cap totals and drops per-unit rows and `log_path`, a test that each new field appears in `tp config --resolved`/`--extract` and is range-validated at both bounds by `tp validate --project`, and a test that `notify_cmd` set in `.tp/config.json` is not resolved while the same key in `.tp/local.json` is.

finding: `file_summary` gains both `truncated` (bool) and `total_changed`, while `total_files` keeps reporting the audited count. `truncated` is exactly `total_changed > total_files`, so one of the two new keys is a stored derivation emitted on every `tp audit` invocation, and test 22 pins both.
suggestion: Emit `total_changed` only and let any consumer derive truncation from `total_changed > total_files`; state that derivation once in REFERENCE.md. (If the bool is kept for `--quiet` robustness, drop `total_changed` instead and name the pre-cap count in the notice only.)
